Hello. My name is Erick Reyna. I'm twenty-four years old and I'm from Monterrey, in the north of Mexico.

I'm a mechatronics student at FIME. It's a big faculty and the classes are hard, but I'm happy there. My favourite subjects are electronics and control.

I'm not married. I live with my family. In my free time I play the guitar — I'm not very good yet, but I practise every week.

My English isn't perfect, but I'm working on it.

9296c73f05160ebc.text:
I get up at six thirty, but I never get up immediately. I usually stay in bed for ten minutes and check my phone.

I have breakfast at seven and I leave the house at seven thirty. I don't drive — I take the bus, because parking at the university is impossible.

My first class starts at eight. On Tuesdays I have four classes and a lab session, so I finish at six in the evening. I sometimes stay longer if the lab isn't finished.

In the evening I study for about two hours. I don't watch much television. On Fridays I play the guitar with a friend, and at the weekend I usually sleep a lot.

010f1ccc64cc0e8e.text:
Our electronics lab is on the second floor, next to the library. It isn't very big, but there is everything we need.

There are ten benches. On each bench there is an oscilloscope, a power supply and a soldering station. There are also two computers at the back, between the window and the door.

The components are in the drawers under the benches. There aren't any resistors in the small cabinet — those are in the storeroom behind the lab.

There are usually about twenty people in the lab in the afternoon. There's only one technician, so sometimes you wait.

616173aaa2026fbb.text:
QUICK START — READ FIRST

Before you begin, check the box. There are four items: the unit, a power cable, a USB cable and this guide. If something is missing, don't use the unit — contact support.

First, connect the power cable. Don't switch it on yet.

Then connect the USB cable to your computer. Wait ten seconds and press the button on the front. The light is orange at first. When it is green, the unit is ready.

You can use the unit without software, but you can't change the settings. To change them, install the application from our website.

Don't open the case. There are no user-serviceable parts inside.

fc013e83bdd46093.text:
Last Monday started badly. My alarm didn't ring, so I woke up at eight instead of six. I ran to the bus stop, but the bus left two minutes before I arrived.

I took a taxi and got to the lab at nine. My supervisor didn't say anything, but he looked at his watch. Then I opened my bag and realised I forgot my laptop at home.

In the end, a colleague lent me an old one and I finished the measurements. I didn't have a good morning, but the afternoon was fine.

9cd71f9ab407adf1.text:
It was almost midnight and we were still working in the lab. Two of us were soldering a board while Ana was writing the test script on her laptop.

Suddenly all the lights went out. The building was completely dark and the only light came from Ana's screen. Nobody was talking; we were all waiting for the emergency lights.

After about a minute, the power came back. We looked at the board and noticed that the microcontroller was hot. While we were checking it, Ana found the problem in her code: the loop never stopped.

We didn't finish that night, but at least we knew what was wrong.

a7662086fd308c86.text:
We had to choose a microcontroller board for the project. There were three options.

The first was the cheapest, but it was also the slowest and it had less memory than the others. The second was slightly more expensive, and it was by far the most popular in the community, which meant more documentation and more examples.

The third was twice as fast as the second, but it cost three times more and it wasn't as well documented.

In the end we chose the second one. It wasn't the best board technically, but it was the most practical for a team of students with a deadline.

5db2a2c0fa839287.text:
Please read this before Thursday.

There isn't much time in the session, so come prepared. You need to bring a few things: a notebook, a calculator and your safety glasses. We have plenty of resistors and capacitors, but there are hardly any jumper wires left, so bring some if you have them.

There is no equipment for individual work — you will share a bench with a partner. If you need any information about the circuit, the datasheet is on the platform.

A piece of advice: read the procedure before you arrive. Students who do this usually finish an hour earlier.

— Yes, I have. I worked in a small startup for two years, from 2022 to 2024. I've also done two internships.

— And have you used our platform?
— Not yet. I've read the documentation, but I haven't built anything with it. I've just started the tutorial, actually.

934d9ff437934bce.text:
Before you enter the laboratory, read these rules carefully.

You must wear safety glasses at all times. You mustn't work alone: there has to be a second person in the room whenever equipment is powered.

You don't have to bring your own tools — the lab provides everything — but you should bring your own notebook, because we don't lend paper.

If you can't finish your measurements in the session, you can book extra time on the platform. However, you are not allowed to stay after nine at night.

If anything smells hot or looks damaged, you must report it immediately. Don't try to repair it yourself.

2e519c6bce8eac50.text:
I joined the automation team in February, so I've been here for about six months now. It's been a strange period.

When I started, I didn't know anything about industrial protocols. I spent the first month reading manuals and I made a lot of mistakes. Since March, though, things have improved a lot. I've commissioned two lines on my own and I haven't caused a single stoppage since May.

The hardest part hasn't been the technology. It's been the language. Most of our documentation is in English, and last week I had to explain a fault to a supplier in Germany by phone. I understood maybe half of what he said.

I've decided to take a certification exam in September. I haven't booked it yet, but I registered for the preparation course on Monday.

fd1523537afbc811.text:
IMPORTANT — READ BEFORE OPERATING

If the temperature rises above 60 °C, the controller shuts down automatically. This is normal behaviour and not a fault.

If you need to run the unit continuously for more than four hours, you will have to install the optional fan kit. Unless the kit is fitted, the warranty does not cover thermal damage.

Some users ask whether they can bypass the thermal cut-out. If we allowed that, the unit would fail within weeks and the repair would cost more than the fan kit. We strongly advise against it.

As long as you keep the vents clear and check the filter monthly, the unit should last around ten years.

795cd89b2e603a31.text:
INCIDENT REPORT — LINE 3

At 14:20 the conveyor was stopped automatically by the safety system. The line had been running normally since the morning shift.

An inspection was carried out immediately. It was found that a proximity sensor had been damaged, probably when a pallet was loaded incorrectly earlier in the day. The sensor was replaced within forty minutes and production was resumed at 15:05.

No injuries were reported. The damaged sensor will be sent to the supplier for analysis.

It has been recommended that operators are given a short refresher on pallet alignment. This recommendation must be approved by the plant manager before it is implemented.

02df2891cb1e33b5.text:
The person who runs our department is an engineer whose career started on the factory floor. She spent eight years as a technician before she studied, which is unusual here and probably explains why she listens to the operators.

The project that gave us the most trouble last year was a retrofit of a line which was installed in 1994. The documentation, which had been written by a company that no longer exists, described a control system nobody recognised.

We eventually found an operator whose father had worked on the original installation. He remembered where the junction boxes were hidden — information that saved us at least three weeks.

40c6de872eab5c90.text:
I couldn't go to the meeting, so Laura told me what happened.

She said the client had rejected the first proposal because it was too expensive. The account manager explained that the price included two years of support, but the client replied that he didn't need it.

Laura told me that our director had asked whether we could deliver a reduced version by November. Nobody answered immediately. Then the lead engineer pointed out that the testing alone would take six weeks, so November was unrealistic.

In the end they agreed that they would send a revised quotation on Friday. Laura warned me that I might have to redo the timeline.

cd4a92c58eb3c297.text:
When I started, I used to spend hours staring at code without understanding anything. I kept changing lines at random and hoping something would work. I remember feeling stupid every single afternoon.

A senior engineer suggested doing something different: instead of guessing, measure. He told me to stop reading the code and start printing values. It sounds obvious now, but at the time I was afraid of looking slow.

I learned to accept that debugging is not about being clever. It's about avoiding assumptions. Now, when something fails, I try to find the smallest case that reproduces it before I try to fix anything.

I still enjoy solving hard problems, but I no longer expect to solve them by staring.

7906a5e049256e70.text:
On Monday we found out that the supplier had called off the delivery. Nobody had pointed out that the purchase order was still unsigned, so we ran out of connectors by Wednesday.

I looked into it and figured out that the approval email had gone to a colleague who left in June. We had to set up a new workflow, which took most of Thursday.

Meanwhile, the client turned down our proposal to put off the demo. They said they had already invited two directors and couldn't cancel.

In the end, my manager came up with a compromise: we would carry out the demo with a partial system and deal with the missing module afterwards. It worked, but I backed up everything three times before I slept.

cb9cbc892d51cb96.text:
Battery choice sounds like a small decision, although it usually determines the whole architecture of a small robot.

Lithium polymer packs are light and deliver high current, which is why almost every competition robot uses them. However, they are unforgiving: a damaged cell can catch fire, and they require a balance charger. Despite these risks, most teams accept them because the weight saving is decisive.

Nickel-metal hydride packs, on the other hand, are heavier and slower to charge. Nevertheless, they tolerate abuse much better and can be stored charged for months without damage. Therefore, they remain a reasonable choice for a first prototype, where the robot spends more time on a bench than in a competition.

In fact, many experienced builders recommend starting with NiMH precisely because the first prototype is the one most likely to be wired backwards.

302a942310ac1182.text:
Looking back, the failure was entirely avoidable.

If we had run the thermal test before the demonstration, we would have seen the drift within twenty minutes. We didn't, because the schedule had already slipped twice and nobody wanted to be the person who delayed it again.

Had the supplier told us that the replacement capacitors came from a different batch, we would probably have retested anyway. They didn't mention it, and to be fair, we never asked.

The most uncomfortable part is this: if I had insisted on the extra week in February, I would not be writing this report now. I did raise it, but I raised it in a meeting where three people were already arguing about something else, and I let it drop.

In hindsight, that was the real failure. Not the capacitors.

7c77c06c84d8b5c9.text:
The board resets roughly every four minutes, which is odd. It can't be a watchdog timeout, because we disabled the watchdog on Tuesday and the behaviour didn't change.

It might be thermal. The regulator does get warm, and four minutes is about how long it takes to reach steady state. On the other hand, if it were thermal, the interval should shorten in a warm room, and it doesn't.

My colleague thinks it must be the power supply. That would account for the regularity, but I'm not convinced: we swapped the supply on Wednesday and nothing improved. He argues that we should have swapped the cable too, which is fair — we needn't have assumed the fault was in the box rather than the wire.

One thing is certain. Whatever it is, it can't have been introduced by the last firmware change, because the resets predate it by a week.

98565e3fb14fd5d7.text:
Before a new supplier is approved, three things have to happen.

First, a sample batch is manufactured and sent to us. We then have the parts measured by an independent laboratory, because measurements taken by the supplier themselves are not accepted, however reliable the supplier is believed to be.

Second, the facility undergoes an audit. This is normally carried out on behalf of several customers at once, which keeps costs down. Suppliers are sometimes said to prefer this arrangement, although in my experience they simply tolerate it.

Third, we have a pilot run produced under normal conditions. Anything made during commissioning is excluded, since it is generally accepted that early units are not representative.

Approval remains subject to annual review. Two suppliers had their approval withdrawn last year, in both cases because documentation had not been kept up to date.

0c7b32f619ebe6e8.text:
Rarely does a first submission require so few changes, and I want to say that clearly before the criticism.

Not only is the methodology sound, but the authors have also released their data, which is still unusual in this field. What impressed me most was the treatment of measurement uncertainty: seldom do papers at this level quantify it honestly.

That said, two issues remain. It is the comparison in section four that concerns me. The baseline was run on different hardware, and no sooner does the text acknowledge this than it moves on. Under no circumstances should such a comparison be presented without a note on the difference.

The second point is minor, namely that three figures lack axis labels.

Notwithstanding these issues, I recommend acceptance with minor revisions. This is, arguably, the most careful paper I have reviewed this year.
